title: 'Ticking Bomb': Ex-Coach Reveals Rohit Sharma's Career-Threatening 2017 Hip Injury
excerpt: Former India S&C coach Soham Desai says Rohit has managed a surgically repaired hip since the 2017 Champions Trophy, needing two strength sessions a week to keep playing at 39.
body:
• Former India strength and conditioning coach Soham Desai has revealed Rohit Sharma suffered a career-threatening hip injury in 2017, around the Champions Trophy final against Pakistan.
  • Rohit underwent surgeries on his hamstring and hip flexor, and his hip remains a weak spot nearly a decade later.
  • Desai said Rohit must complete at least two strength sessions a week — without them, he is 'a red flag, a ticking bomb'.
  • At 39, Rohit remains India's ODI opener and has stated his intention to play the 2027 ODI World Cup.

Rohit Sharma has played the last eight years of his career managing a hip injury that could have ended it. Former India strength and conditioning coach Soham Desai has revealed that Rohit suffered a career-threatening injury around his hip in 2017 and underwent surgeries on his hamstring and hip flexor, pushing back against the long-running criticism that the former India captain is lazy and does not train.

Speaking on a podcast with Prashant Desai, Soham Desai — who worked with the Indian team for nearly five years — said the injury dates to the 2017 Champions Trophy in England, where India lost the final to Pakistan, according to NDTV Sports.

"So people say this Rohit is lazy, mota hai (he's fat), training nahi karta hai (doesn't train). People need to understand this: Rohit Sharma had a career-threatening injury around his hip in 2017. So he has got surgeries in his hamstring and his hip flexor and all that."

— Soham Desai, former India strength and conditioning coach

Two sessions a week, non-negotiable

Desai explained that the area around Rohit's hip remains his weak spot, and that managing it has required a fixed weekly routine for the better part of a decade. "Around his hip is his weak spot. If he doesn't train for a minimum of two strength sessions in a week, he is a red flag, he is a ticking bomb. And that is the scenario for the last seven to eight years," he said, in comments also reported by Khelja and Circle of Cricket.

"Forget about scoring runs, leading in the IPL, playing twelve months, all formats. For the last seven-eight years, it has been non-negotiable. Either he has to do that or he has to work in a particular manner on the ground. Without those two, he cannot last — and this is not a secret. It is in the public domain," Desai added. His conclusion was blunt: if Rohit had actually been lazy, he would not have lasted at the top level until today.

The fitness debate around a 39-year-old opener

Rohit's fitness has been a recurring subject of scrutiny on social media, where his physique is routinely mocked and his training questioned. Desai's account reframes that debate: the batter's body has required more structured work, not less, than most of his contemporaries, because the margin for error around his hip is so small.

The stakes are current, not historical. Rohit, 39, now plays only ODI cricket for India and remains a vital part of the batting line-up, producing impactful knocks in recent months. He has made his intention clear to represent India at the 2027 ODI World Cup — by which time he will be around 40 — and is expected to feature in India's upcoming ODI series against New Zealand. Whether his body holds up until that tournament is, on Desai's telling, a question that will be answered week by week, two strength sessions at a time.

What it means for India's World Cup planning

For India's selectors, Desai's revelation underlines why Rohit's workload has been managed in blocks and why his availability is planned around recovery windows rather than assumed. A player whose hip is a permanent 'red flag' risk cannot be treated like a 25-year-old opener, however well he is batting. It also explains the longevity itself: nearly two decades into an international career that began in 2007, Rohit is still opening for India — not in spite of the work behind the scenes, but because of it.
